title: Why is the United States so powerful?
subtitle: Birth of a superpower
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: A country that did not exist 250 years ago now decides almost everything, almost everywhere. Two oceans, a bomb, a dollar and a pair of jeans: how the United States became the first superpower.
author: ivana-toskovic

hero.hook: A country that did not exist 250 years ago, and whose decisions now weigh on the whole planet.

blocks.text: The United States is a young state. It was born on **July 4, 1776**, when thirteen British colonies declared their independence. Today the federal union has **50 states**, with very unequal levels of development. Yet the country ranks in the world's top three, both by population and by land area.

Geography is its first asset. Bordered by the Atlantic and the Pacific, the territory is protected by two natural barriers: for a long time, the country did not have to invest heavily in its own defense. Fertile land, oil and steel fed rapid growth, which took off after World War II. That is when the United States was called a [[superpower]] for the first time.

sections.title: 1945: the army, the bomb and the dollar

blocks.text: For the United States, timing was everything. In **1945**, the countries of Europe came out of the war weakened in every way. The Americans came out stronger than ever: nuclear weapons, a gigantic army, aircraft carriers, then intercontinental ballistic missiles. This militarization gave them influence on a global scale.

blocks.caption: Delegates at the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944, which gave birth to the IMF.

blocks.text: Money followed the weapons. The **dollar** became the currency of international trade and of the big institutions created at the time, such as the [[International Monetary Fund]]. [[NATO]], the military alliance founded with the countries of Western Europe, wove a web of allies across the continent. Financial power and military power reinforced each other. For the rest of the world, the mix was convincing: many countries began to long for that kind of stability.

sections.title: The American dream and soft power

blocks.text: The United States has always been associated with the [[American dream]]: a country where everything is possible. Millions of immigrants landed there, drawn by those possibilities. Their energy fed a complete system of development: industry and technology, but also research, education, diplomacy and, later, software.

blocks.caption: European immigrants arriving at Ellis Island, in New York harbor, in the early 20th century.

blocks.text: The American political scientist [[Joseph Nye]] gave this power of attraction a name: [[soft power]]. Alongside military force, or hard power, a country also dominates through the appeal of its culture and its ideas. After the [[Cold War]], this soft power became the cornerstone of American dominance.

The term soft power first appeared in 1990, in an article by Joseph Nye in the journal Foreign Policy, just as the Cold War was ending. Its everyday face was simpler: everybody wanted to drink Coca-Cola and wear jeans.

sections.title: Why not London, Beijing or Moscow?

blocks.text: Why the United States, and not another power? Because every rival had a weak spot. **Britain** was a global power, highly developed, with the greatest navy in the world. But its population and territory could not measure up to the sheer size of the United States.

**China**, a far older nation, had a giant population and a great economy, but at the time it lacked military capacity. **Russia** had the territory, the natural resources and a long military history; it was weak, however, in financial terms. During the Cold War, as the Soviet Union, it still managed to stand up to the United States. Its overextension, on too many fronts at once, was one of the reasons it lost its position.

sections.title: Hollywood, Google, Ivy League: a universal attraction

blocks.text: The English language, McDonald's, Hollywood, the great universities of the [[Ivy League]]: all of this built the position of superpower. Soft power works neither by threat nor by reward. Others simply want what you want. The appeal of American-style liberal democracy shaped the global scene, and the rise of **Google**, **Amazon** and **Apple** made that presence permanent.

blocks.caption: The Hollywood sign in the hills of Los Angeles: American cinema is exported all over the world.

blocks.text: Other nations can confront the United States, but none can match that attractiveness. Chinese language and religion remain too different from the rest of the world; Russia leans toward raw force and hierarchy. India and Brazil are in the same situation. None of these powers has what the United States offers: a form of universality.

Protected by two oceans, enriched by its resources, armed and funded like no one else after 1945, the United States rules above all through the appeal of its way of life: soft power is what makes the superpower.

sources.text: J. S. Nye, « Soft Power », Foreign Policy, n° 80, 1990, p. 153-171.
